title: Adjective order and -ed/-ing adjectives
titleVi: Trật tự tính từ và tính từ đuôi -ed/-ing
summary: Xếp đúng thứ tự tính từ và chọn đúng -ed/-ing — hai lỗi nhỏ làm câu mất tự nhiên ngay.
whyItMatters: Người đọc bản xứ không nghĩ về quy tắc trật tự tính từ, nhưng họ **cảm nhận** ngay khi nó sai: *a wooden beautiful desk* nghe lệch tai dù hiểu nghĩa. Tương tự, *I am boring* khiến bạn tự nhận mình nhàm chán. Hai lỗi này xuất hiện dày trong Writing Task 1 và Speaking, và sửa được chúng là cách rẻ nhất để câu văn nghe tự nhiên hơn.

sections.heading: The order native readers expect
body: When several adjectives come before a noun, English orders them by category: **opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose**. A useful example is *a beautiful large old rectangular brown Italian wooden dining table* — absurd in real use, but it shows the sequence.

In practice you rarely need more than two or three. The important contrast is **opinion before fact**: *a lovely old house*, never *an old lovely house*. Opinion adjectives (beautiful, useful, terrible, impressive) tell us what you think; the others tell us what the thing **is**.
A second habit matters just as much: putting the **most informative** adjective closest to the noun. *A steel bridge* is more useful than *a big bridge* when the material is the point.

sections.heading: Two adjectives are usually enough
body: Academic writing rewards precision, not accumulation. *A severe housing shortage* beats *a very bad, big, serious housing shortage*: one strong adjective plus one factual one carries the meaning.
When you use two, keep the order opinion + fact (*a chronic labour shortage*, *an ambitious national plan*) or fact + fact in the standard sequence (*a rapidly ageing rural population*).

Adjectives also follow linking verbs — **be, seem, look, feel, become, remain** — and come after indefinite pronouns: *something useful*, *nothing new*, *anyone interested*. This is where Vietnamese learners often insert the adjective before the pronoun: *useful something* is not English.

examples.right: The city faces a severe shortage of affordable housing.
examples.wrong: The city faces an affordable severe shortage of housing.
examples.note: Opinion (*severe*) comes before the descriptive *affordable*… but here *affordable housing* is a fixed compound, so keep it together after the noun.

examples.right: They live in a cramped old flat near the station.
Is there anything interesting in the report?
examples.wrong: Is there interesting anything in the report?

sections.heading: -ed or -ing? Who feels, who causes
body: The rule is short: **-ed** describes how a person or thing **feels**; **-ing** describes the person or thing that **causes** the feeling. *The lecture was boring* (it caused boredom) → *I was bored* (I felt it).
This is why *I am boring* is a genuine insult: it means you make other people bored. Say *I am bored* if you feel uninterested.
The same pair runs through the whole academic vocabulary: *interested/interesting*, *concerned/concerning*, *alarmed/alarming*, *satisfied/satisfying*, *confused/confusing*, *exhausted/exhausting*.

rows: a concerning trend in youth unemployment
a satisfying solution to the housing problem

sections.heading: Adjectives for groups and for emphasis
body: **The + adjective** names a whole group: *the elderly*, *the unemployed*, *the wealthy*, *the homeless*. It takes a plural verb: *The unemployed **are** entitled to support.*
This structure is efficient in Task 2 because it lets you talk about a social category without repeating *people who are…*: *Governments must protect **the vulnerable** during energy transitions.*
Avoid turning it into a noun with a singular meaning. *The poor* is a group; one person is *a poor person*, not *a poor*.

examples.right: The elderly are more vulnerable to extreme heat.
examples.wrong: The elderly is more vulnerable to extreme heat.
examples.note: **The + adjective** for a group takes a plural verb.

examples.right: Rising rents have hit the young hardest.
examples.note: A group reading — natural in IELTS conclusions.

examples.right: A concerning number of graduates remain unemployed a year after leaving university.

commonMistakes.wrong: They bought a wooden beautiful dining table.
commonMistakes.right: They bought a beautiful wooden dining table.
commonMistakes.why: Tính từ **opinion** (beautiful) luôn đứng trước tính từ **material** (wooden). Người Việt thường đặt từ mô tả vật chất gần danh từ vì tiếng Việt nói *bàn ăn bằng gỗ đẹp*.

commonMistakes.wrong: I am boring because the film was too long.
commonMistakes.right: I am bored because the film was too long.
commonMistakes.why: **-ing** nói thứ gây ra cảm giác; **-ed** nói người cảm nhận. *I am boring* = tôi làm người khác chán.
Bài giảng không thể cảm thấy chán; nó gây ra sự chán. Vật/sự việc thường đi với `-ing`.

commonMistakes.wrong: The government should support the poor people more.
commonMistakes.right: The government should support the poor more.
commonMistakes.why: **The + adjective** đã bao hàm *people*, nên *the poor people* là lặp. Nếu muốn nhấn mạnh, dùng *poor households* hoặc *people on low incomes*.

commonMistakes.wrong: There is interesting something in the report.
commonMistakes.right: There is something interesting in the report.
commonMistakes.why: Tính từ đứng **sau** các đại từ *something, anything, nothing, everything*.

ieltsTips: Trong Task 1, chỉ dùng **hai** tính từ cho một danh từ: một tính từ đánh giá + một tính từ dữ liệu. *A marked upward trend*, *a modest annual increase* — vừa đủ để giám khảo thấy bạn kiểm soát được trật tự.
Dùng cặp `-ed/-ing` để mô tả phản ứng của xã hội, rất tự nhiên trong Task 2: *an **alarming** rise in screen time*, *a **concerning** level of youth debt*, *a **convincing** case for regulation*.
Khi mô tả một nhóm người, dùng `the + adjective` để câu gọn và học thuật: *the elderly*, *the unemployed*, *the vulnerable*. Nhớ động từ số nhiều: *The unemployed **are** …*
Đừng nhồi ba tính từ trước một danh từ. Một tính từ mạnh đúng chỗ (*a chronic shortage*) ghi điểm hơn ba tính từ yếu xếp hàng.

exercises.question: They moved into a ___ house near the river.
The documentary was so ___ that half the class fell asleep.
exercises.explanation: The documentary **causes** boredom → **-ing**. *Bored* describes the audience.

exercises.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: The elderly is more at risk during heatwaves.
The elderly are more at risk during heatwaves.
The elderlies are more at risk during heatwaves.
Elderly are more at risk during heatwaves.
exercises.explanation: **The + adjective** for a group takes a plural verb and has no plural -s.

exercises.question: I was ___ to hear that the scholarship had been cut.
Choose the natural order.
exercises.explanation: size → colour → material: *a small grey concrete office*.

exercises.question: The rise in youth unemployment is deeply ___ (concern).
Many graduates feel ___ (frustrate) by the shortage of entry-level jobs.
They live in a ___ (beautiful / old / Italian) villa outside the city.
Is there ___ (anything / useful) in the appendix?
The charity provides legal advice to ___ (homeless).
exercises.explanation: **The homeless** names the group; no noun is needed.
